Figure 38. Von Mises stress distribution in the tank wall during 27 days of preheating followed by a few hours of tank filling. The corresponding von Mises stress on the tank floor during the 27 days of preheating followed by some hours of tank filling is shown in Figure 37. As shown in this figure, the maximum stresses are located in the welding zones, with higher values typically observed at the intersection between short-edge and long-edge welds, influenced by the residual stress remaining after fabrication. A significant stress relaxation is observed as the tank floor heats up. The observed residual stress relaxation on the order of 50 – 60% is attributed to flow stress drop as a function of temperature; relaxation due to creep is expected to be negligible at the temperatures and time scales modelled. Even after this relaxation, the operational stress values remain high enough to potentially produce premature failures in molten salt tanks, similar to the findings of the previously published lifetime analysis [4]. 32 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Similarly, the von Mises stresses in the tank wall are presented in Figure 38 for the preheating and initial tank fill process. Unlike the tank floor, stress variations in the wall are observed over the 27 days of preheating. During preheating and tank filling, both the wall and the floor deform. These deformations are less critical in the tank wall, as it has greater freedom to expand or contract than the floor, which is highly restricted. The evolution of the floor deformation distribution is presented in Figure 39. The deformation pattern is highly dependent on the initial plastic deformation of the floor after welding fabrication. During preheating, the temperature increases slowly to ensure more homogeneous heating of the tank and to avoid large deformations.
